lesson.title: Tying Voltage, Current, and Resistance Together
lesson.summary: Ohm's Law shows how voltage, current, and resistance are locked together in a single proportional relationship, and gives you the tool to calculate any one of them from the other two.
lesson.body:
You already know what each of these three quantities means on its own: voltage is the push that drives charge through a circuit, current is how much charge actually flows per unit time, and resistance is whatever opposes that flow. Ohm's Law is the statement that connects all three into one precise relationship: $V = IR$. It tells you that the voltage across a conductor is exactly equal to the current passing through it multiplied by its resistance. This isn't just a formula to memorize ,  it's a description of cause and effect. Voltage is the cause that forces current to move, and resistance determines how much current results from a given amount of push.

Think about why this makes physical sense. If you increase the voltage across a fixed resistor, you're increasing the force driving charge along, so more current flows ,  voltage and current rise together when resistance stays the same. On the other hand, if you keep the voltage fixed but increase the resistance, you're making it harder for charge to move, so the current has to drop. Ohm's Law captures both of these behaviors in one equation: current is directly proportional to voltage, and inversely proportional to resistance. You can see this by rearranging the formula into $I = V/R$, which reads naturally as "current equals how hard you're pushing divided by how much is resisting."

A concrete example makes this easier to hold onto. Suppose you have a resistor rated at 10 ohms, and you connect it across a 5-volt source. Using $I = V/R$, the current through that resistor is $5\text{ V} / 10\ \Omega = 0.5\text{ A}$. Now imagine you swap in a 20-ohm resistor but keep the same 5-volt source. The current drops to $5/20 = 0.25\text{ A}$ ,  doubling the resistance cut the current in half, exactly as you'd expect from the inverse relationship. If instead you doubled the voltage to 10 volts while keeping the original 10-ohm resistor, the current would double back up to 1 A. Every one of these outcomes falls directly out of the same equation; you're just solving for a different unknown each time.

It's worth being precise about what Ohm's Law is really describing: a relationship between the voltage across a specific component and the current through that same component, given its resistance. If you know any two of the three quantities for a component, you can always solve for the third by rearranging the equation ,  $V = IR$, $I = V/R$, or $R = V/I$. This flexibility is what makes Ohm's Law such a workhorse: whether you're given a resistor's rating and the current flowing through it, or a voltage source and a resistance, you can always find the missing piece.

One subtlety to keep in mind is that Ohm's Law assumes the resistance stays constant for the range of voltage and current you're working with. Many resistors used in basic circuits behave this way over normal operating conditions, which is exactly why this simple linear relationship is so useful as a starting point. As you move into analyzing full circuits with multiple components, this same equation applied component by component becomes the foundation for almost every calculation you'll do.
